digest.intro: Chips, singularities, soft tissue, and a 75-cent accounting error that caught a spy.

items.title: Z.ai Confirms Ox Alpha: Another Chinese Open-Weight Model Rival to DeepSeek
items.blurb: Z.ai is releasing weights for Ox Alpha, a model that was built quietly and benchmarks alongside DeepSeek. The structural story here isn't any single model — it's that Chinese labs are now systematically choosing open-weight releases as a geopolitical and ecosystem move, compounding pressure on Western closed-model incumbents.

items.title: OpenAI Jalapeño: A First-Gen Inference Chip That Actually Beats Nvidia
items.blurb: OpenAI went from hiring the chip team to manufacturing tape-out in 16 months — an almost unheard-of ASIC development cycle — and the resulting chip benchmarks 1.5–1.9× better than Nvidia Blackwell on performance per watt across multiple open-source models. The surprising architectural choice: it's deliberately generalized, not overfit to OpenAI's own models, which is what makes it dangerous for Nvidia long-term rather than just a one-trick internal tool.

items.title: Apple M6 and M5 Ultra: 2nm, Quad-Die, 1.2TB/s
items.blurb: M6 is Apple's first 2-nanometer chip and ships a Dual 16-core Neural Engine alongside 170GB/s unified memory bandwidth — the number that matters most for large local model inference. M5 Ultra goes further with a quad-die UltraFusion architecture delivering 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth, 50% more than M3 Ultra, which means the Mac Studio is now a plausible local inference node for serious generative workloads.

items.title: C2PA Cameras Do Not Survive Contact with Reality
items.blurb: The cryptographic image-provenance standard meant to distinguish real photos from AI fakes relies on Android's Key Attestation — which breaks the moment a device is rooted, and one-click root exploits now exist for fully-patched Pixel phones in the wild. The researcher reported this 90 days before publishing; the standard's trust model has no realistic patch path because hardware vulnerabilities in existing devices can't be updated.

items.title: Black Hole Singularity Is a Surface, Not a Point
items.blurb: Two observers falling into a Schwarzschild black hole along different angular trajectories don't meet at the singularity — they lose causal contact well before reaching it, which means the singularity has spatial extent, not a point geometry. The paper's further implication for quantum gravity: the quantum states of a black hole probably reside at this effectively 2-dimensional singular surface, co-evolving with the trapped Hawking radiation inside the event horizon.

items.title: 450-Million-Year-Old Soft Tissue, Preserved in Pyrite
items.blurb: A crinoid fossil from before animals had fully colonized dry land — and more than 200 million years before the first dinosaur — has its tube feet intact, crystallized into pyrite so fast by bacteria that they outran decay. This is only the second time soft tissue has ever been found in a crinoid fossil, out of millions examined.

items.title: Rheoscopic Fluid: Reject Simulation, Return to Mica
items.blurb: Mica flakes suspended in water with a drop of soap self-align with fluid shear, making flow structure directly visible — a cheap, tactile alternative to computational fluid dynamics for anyone who wants to see what's actually happening in a flow rather than render it. The linked video starts with a miniature ship hull moved through a thin fluid sandwich between laser-cut acrylic sheets, and escalates toward coffee-table-scale sand-drawing mechanisms.

items.title: Stalking the Wily Hacker: 40 Years Later — Cliff Stoll
items.blurb: In 1986, Cliff Stoll noticed a 75-cent accounting discrepancy in his university's computer system and spent the next year obsessively tracking it to a KGB-connected hacker ring — the original slow-burn infosec investigation. Stoll recounts it with the energy of a man who still can't believe it happened, and the talk is less about hacking than about the obsessive naturalist mindset: following one small wrong thing until the whole system reveals itself.

facts.fact: OpenAI's Jalapeño chip went from initial team hiring to manufacturing tape-out in approximately 16 months — an unusually fast ASIC development cycle even by aggressive industry standards.
A researcher found image manipulations — the kind that would trigger academic retraction — in marketing materials for over 17,000 commercially sold antibodies used in biomedical research.

Two observers falling into a black hole along different angular paths lose causal contact with each other well before reaching the singularity — meaning the singularity itself is spatially extended, not a geometric point.
The 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil is only the second time soft tissue has ever been found preserved in any crinoid fossil, out of millions examined worldwide.

Apple's M5 Ultra uses a quad-die UltraFusion architecture delivering 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth — 50% more than M3 Ultra — making the Mac Studio a credible local inference platform for large models.

make_something.prompt: Build a rheoscopic fluid panel: a thin fluid layer sandwiched between two sheets of laser-cut or cut acrylic, seeded with cosmetic mica flakes and a drop of dish soap. Mount a small object — a hull cross-section, a wing profile, an abstract form — on a magnet beneath the bottom sheet so you can drag it through the fluid and watch the shear lines appear. Try filming it at high contrast under a single raking light source. The mica aligns with flow, so you're not illustrating fluid dynamics — you're directly reading them in a physical medium.

art_picks.title: Mauvais Sang
art_picks.creator: Leos Carax
art_picks.why: A film that runs on pure system — youth culture, ritual, forbidden knowledge, bodies in space — where the visual grammar IS the argument. Carax builds a world where every gesture is already a symbol before it's an action, and the famous running sequence is one of cinema's most expressive feedback loops between music, motion, and longing.

art_picks.title: Alamar (To the Sea)
art_picks.creator: Tomás Saraceno
art_picks.why: Saraceno builds cosmologies — spider webs mapped as load-bearing architecture, ecosystems as social contracts, the invisible physics of air as political space. His practice is the exact category-blur you want: ecological systems as aesthetic objects, science as myth-making, the studio as research lab.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: The rare record that functions less as music than as a revealed system — pure texture organized by logic you can feel but not name, the sonic equivalent of generative 3D before it had a name. Still the high-water mark for the idea that constraint + obsession = atmosphere.

events.name: Christian Rutledge: An Inch of This New York Mile — Opening
events.why: A lower-profile gallery opening from an artist deep in the city-as-system territory — the title alone signals the kind of obsessive, granular urban attention worth showing up for.

events.name: Book Launch: You Weren't There — '90s Graffiti in New York
events.why: Printed Matter is the right room for this — a deep archive of a frontier culture (NYC graffiti in the 90s) before it hardened into brand, exactly the kind of scene-before-institution moment that reveals how social systems form and calcify.

events.name: Jody Pinto: Body/Land Exchange — Opening
events.why: Pinto works at the literal edge of body and terrain — her practice maps the body as landscape and landscape as body, a physical/conceptual feedback loop that sits right at Willem's intersection of systems and the tactile.

events.name: Opening Celebration: Camille Henrot — Dogs
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (5th Ave & 60th St), Manhattan
events.why: Henrot's dog sculptures are a precise inquiry into domestication, etiquette, and societal rule-making — playful objects doing serious systems work at the entrance to Central Park; free, public, and opens with a celebration 6–7pm.
